subject: Stan model cache on the Net (speeding up "compile" time)

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Stan model cache on the Net (speeding up "compile" time)
parts:
Hi,

It occurs to me that there aren't that many Stan models out there in
heavy use (esp. in the classroom). Ignoring variable name permutations
and ordering perhaps there are about 500 that account for ~90% of use?
Why not just compile them all in advance and serve them to users in
binary form, à la CRAN or PyPI? Imagine how happy users would be if all
example and textbook models "compiled" in 2 seconds.

Here are some numbers: a very simple model takes 47 seconds to compile
on my computer but with my very slow internet connection it takes ~10
seconds to download the saved model (20M) from a server in New Jersey.
I bet on fiber one could download the model in 2 seconds. And fiber is
only going to get cheaper. Both R and Python have a mechanism for
packaging up a model that's already in use when people save a model to
disk.

Best,

Allen

p.s. Yes, a model would have to be compiled for each architecture ---
PyPI already does this with its binary "wheels". And one would have to
cryptographically sign the models. (One could package the public key in
the source code.)

users would no longer need to have a C++ compiler available if they had
an internet connection available---again, provided the cache were
suitably large (>1,000 models) and Stan models were made invariant to
variable ordering and variable name permutations.

Best,

Allen

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan model cache on the Net (speeding up "compile" time)
parts:
On 03/28, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What are you imagining those 1000 models are?
> And how would people find them?
>

In the social sciences the range of models used isn't that broad. I
suppose I'm just assuming that a significant chunk of our users are
implementing models that already exist (e.g., the horseshoe or a model
from a well-known paper in their field). One could also scrape the web,
github, and stan-users and compile every valid Stan model ever seen
there. Storage and bandwidth are cheap and getting cheaper.

> We couldn't put this out in an official (CRAN) R
> package because of storage and build-time constraints
> for packages.

Right, we'd have to use our own infrastructure. I think this could be
cheap(ish). At its simplest it could just be a static directory serving
files where the filename is the SHA256 hash of the compiled .hpp for the
model.

I can prototype this in PyStan this summer I think. It would be easier
if we did the RStan/PyStan API refactor first though.

Best,

Allen

For ecologists you could also make the transition to Stan easier just from having standard GLMM's, 'animal models', and mark-recapture models that are specified by model matrix (from R and Python). messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stan model cache on the Net (speeding up "compile" time)
parts:
Progress on making precompiled models easy to deploy would
be great.  I don't know who uses them --- for me, the benefit
of Stan is being able to customize a model.

+\infty

When building a model with someone new to stats in almost
all cases the most excited part is when they get to adjust the
model to their science instead of an arbitrary model.  Making
it easy for people to not have to think about their model does
no one any good (unless people can use precompiled models
for only three months and then we cut them off or charge them,
in which case we retain the incentive of easy entry without the
cost of people falling into routine models).

I don't think we disagree at all! I imagine the fetching of the
precompiled model would be completely transparent to the user---the
model is just identified by the hash of the model's C++ code. The cache
could hold 100,000+ distinct models. And of course if it's an unseen
model, you'd use the compiler (or, someday, have a nice, fast machine
compile it on demand in the cloud and add it to the cache). A side
benefit would be that we would know (via traffic stats) what models were
being used most often.

Model compile time is the only issue being addressed here.

Best,

Allen

While we could afford the storage of 100K * 10MB (that's
still only 1TB), it would present a difficult organization
problem. I'm uncomfortable officially distributing models
that we don't vet.

One place to start would be to go through the BUGS models and
make sure they're all up to our recommended practices.
That'll get us up to about 75 or something like that. Then
repeat 1500 times :-)

- Bob

The barrier for me contributing standardized models (in addition to time) is that there's no clear standard to follow... and so far no easy framework for vetting that a pile of models works.
